title: Lending and the cost of a broken promise
blurb: What you take on when you lend money, and why a bigger promise is not a bonus.
t1.title: Lending and borrowing
t1.hook: A shop owner asks {n} neighbours for {amt} each. He promises to pay back {amtBack} after a year. Your mission: understand what each neighbour is signing up for.
t1.define: A **borrower** uses someone else's money and pays interest for it. A **lender** gives the money and earns that interest.
t1.formula: Interest for one year = amount lent × rate. Write the rate as a decimal. Example: lending ₹2,000 at 5% for a year earns 2,000 × 0.05 = ₹100.
t1.note: A bank deposit is a loan that you give to the bank. In both cases you are the lender.
q1.prompt: When you keep money in a bank deposit, who is the lender?
q1.opt.d: Nobody, because it is not a loan
q1.hint: Who hands over the money, and who uses it?
q1.explain: You hand your money to the bank to use, so you are the lender.
q2.prompt: A shop owner borrows {b1} and promises {r1} interest for one year. How much interest does he owe? Type a number in rupees.
q2.hint: Work out {r1} of the amount borrowed.
t2.title: The promise
t2.steps.2: The shop promises {amtBack} back after a year
t2.steps.3: If the shop pays, each neighbour earns {gain}, which is a return of {rate}
q3.prompt: A lender hands over {l2}. The borrower promises {l2back} back. If the promise is kept, what is the lender's return? Type a percentage.
q3.hint: Return = what you earn ÷ what you lent. First find what you earn.
q3.explain: {l2back} minus {l2} is the profit. Divided by {l2}, that is a return of {ret}.
q4.prompt: All {n} neighbours are paid in full. How much interest does the shop owner pay in total? Type a number in rupees.
q4.hint: Use the interest for one neighbour from the steps, then count all {n}.
t3.title: When the borrower cannot pay
t3.define: **Default** is when a borrower cannot pay what was promised. Lenders may get back only part of their money, or none.
t3.steps.1: The shop has a bad year and closes
t3.steps.2: The owner can repay only part of what he owes
t3.steps.3: Each lender gets back less than they lent
t3.explore: Open the lab. One lender lends money. Change the promised rate and how much comes back if the shop fails.
q5.prompt: In the lab, set the money recovered to {rec40} and leave the rate alone. If the shop fails, what is the lender's net result? Use a minus sign for a loss.
q5.hint: Net result = money that comes back minus the money lent. Read it from the failing side of the lab.
q5.explain: Only {rec40} of {labAmt} comes back, so the lender is down by {labLoss}. The net result is {labNet}.
q6.prompt: Now set the promised rate to {r20}. If the shop pays, how much interest does the lender earn? Type a number in rupees.
q6.hint: Read interest earned from the paying side of the lab.
q7.prompt: Move the promised rate up and down while the shop fails. Does a higher promised rate change the loss?
q7.opt.a: No. The loss depends on how much is recovered
q7.opt.b: Yes. A higher rate always protects the lender
q7.opt.c: Yes. A higher rate makes the loss bigger
q7.opt.d: Only when the lender is rich
q7.hint: Watch the failing side of the lab as you move the rate slider.
q7.explain: If the shop fails, a promise is just a promise. The loss depends on what is recovered, not on the rate that was promised.
t4.title: A higher promise is a warning
t4.tradeoff: A higher promised rate usually means a higher chance that the promise breaks. A safer borrower usually offers less, and sleeps easier.
t4.mistake: A very high promised return is not a free bonus. It is often a warning sign. No one can truly guarantee a return.
q8.prompt: Neighbour A has run a shop for 20 years and promises 8%. A stranger, B, promises 40% a year, guaranteed. How should you think about B?
q8.opt.a: The higher promise signals higher risk, so look much closer
q8.opt.b: 40% is a bonus, so B is the better choice
q8.opt.d: Only the rate matters, not who is borrowing
q8.fb.b: A very high promise is more often a sign of danger than of a bonus. Someone safe rarely needs to offer so much.
q8.fb.c: The word guaranteed is only a promise. No borrower can remove the chance of failing.
q8.hint: Ask why anyone would offer to pay so much.
q8.explain: A promise far above the normal rate is a warning. A promise is not a guarantee.
q9.prompt: Challenge: you lend {l5}. The borrower fails and repays only {rec40} of it. How many rupees do you lose? Type a number.
q9.hint: Work out the part that is not repaid.
q9.explain: Only {rec40} of {l5} comes back, so you lose {loss5}.
t5.title: Where lending shows up
t5.note: A bank deposit is a loan to a bank. A bond is a loan to a company or the government. In each case you are the lender, and the promise can break.
q10.opt.a: Keeping money in a bank deposit
q10.opt.b: Buying a share in a company
q10.hint: Look for the one where you hand over money and expect it back with interest.
q10.explain: A deposit is a loan to the bank. A share is ownership, gold is a thing, and a bill is a payment.
q11.opt.b: The borrower cannot pay what was promised
q11.opt.c: The lender raises the interest rate
q11.hint: Think about the shop that closed.
q11.explain: Default is when a borrower cannot pay what was promised.
glossary.borrower.def: Someone who uses another person's money and pays interest.
glossary.lender.def: Someone who gives money to be used and earns interest.
glossary.default.def: When a borrower cannot pay what was promised.
